problem: Existing 3D house simulators either support navigation only, with no interaction (MINOS, House3D, DeepMind Lab, Matterport3D), or support manipulation with limits. HoME only allows moving objects, and AI2-THOR at the time was restricted to a single room. None combined multi-room house navigation with rich manipulation: pick and place, opening and closing containers, and toggling appliance state.
motivation: Training neural agent policies needs interactive environments that give large amounts of feedback, and physical robots are costly and hard to scale. Tasks that combine language, vision and planning need scenes where language must resolve specific object instances among duplicates via spatial relations, where objects can be hidden inside containers (forcing exploration), and where partial first-person observability demands memory.
key_idea: Build a Unity-based, cross-platform, multi-room house simulator (58 rooms in 10 houses, 150 object types) in which a first-person agent can navigate continuously between rooms and manipulate objects and the environment: pick and place, open and close containers, and toggle object states. Deliberately populate rooms with many same-type objects so that instructions must rely on spatial and attribute grounding.
insight: This is a pure environment paper with no experiments or ablations. Its lesson lies in the design rationale. Duplicate object instances per room (e.g., many towels or plates) force instructions like 'the yellow towel left of the sink' and prevent word-to-object shortcuts. Openable containers make goals such as 'the glass from the cupboard' require relation resolution, exploration across candidate containers and multi-step planning. Egocentric partial observability requires memory. Its niche versus related simulators: whole multi-room houses (vs. single-room THOR at the time) and state toggling plus container manipulation (vs. HoME's move-only interaction).
method: Scene content: 58 rooms organized into 10 houses of 4-7 rooms each (bathrooms, bedrooms, kitchens, ...); 150 object types textured into 330 distinct objects, about 30 objects per room on average.

Interaction model: 71 manipulable types, of which 60 are pick-and-place, 6 open/close (containers such as dishwashers and cabinets that can hold objects, e.g., dishwasher racks) and 5 state-changing (e.g., faucet, TV power); simple physics with collision detection and gravity.

Agent and action space: first-person view with position given by 2 location and 2 orientation coordinates; continuous actions that can be discretized to a chosen step size: move-forward/back, strafe-left/right, look-left/right/up/down (look-up/down also close/open an engaged container) and a single context-dependent 'interact' action (engage container, pick, drop, toggle).

Evaluation protocol: agent behavior is compared with an annotated demonstration of states and actions. Navigation error is the sum of per-room straight-line distances through doors to the goal. Manipulation accuracy is the F1 between the ordered interaction-action lists extracted from agent and reference; placements within 1.0 m of the target in the same room count as correct.

Implementation: Unity 3D with C# logic, compiled for Linux, MacOS, Windows, Android, iOS and WebGL. Three modes: standalone (keyboard/mouse, WebGL crowdsourcing, trajectory saved), simulator (replays saved trajectories) and client (socket API for ML frameworks returning observations, reward/feedback and object state).

Programmatic scenario generation: objects can be added, removed or re-placed at runtime using annotated per-room surface locations (type, orientation, target surface, coordinates) without reloading; new assets can be imported from the Unity Asset Store.

setting.training_data: none (no agent trained; environment supports crowdsourced demonstrations via WebGL)
setting.observation: egocentric first-person rendered view (agent sees only what is in front of it); API also exposes object positions/states
setting.action_space: continuous (discretizable) move-forward/back, strafe-left/right, look-left/right/up/down, interact (pick/drop/open-close container/toggle)

numbers_note: No experimental results: the paper describes the simulator, its evaluation metrics and a qualitative comparison table with other simulators; no agents or baselines are evaluated.
results: There are no quantitative results. The contribution is the CHALET environment: 58 rooms and 10 houses, 150 object types / 330 objects, 71 manipulable types, continuous navigation across rooms plus container and state manipulation. It also proposes navigation-error and manipulation-F1 metrics against annotated demonstrations. A qualitative table positions it against MINOS, House3D, AI2-THOR, Matterport3D, HoME and DeepMind Lab as one of the few simulators offering both navigation and manipulation.
limitations: Small scale (58 rooms, 10 default houses) compared with thousands of houses in House3D, MINOS and HoME, which limits generalization studies.
Synthetic Unity-rendered scenes with simple physics rather than photorealistic or real-scan environments.
No task dataset, baseline agents or experiments are reported; evaluation relies on annotated demonstrations that are not described.
